evidence.claim: Article 104 vests executive authority in the President, including national-security policy, treaty ratification, appointment and dismissal of ministers and senior officials, military-use decisions, and presidential decrees subject to legal limits; Article 116 lets the TBMM or the President renew elections; Article 105 sets a parliamentary investigation path.
evidence.title: Anayasa | Anayasa Mahkemesi
evidence.excerpt: Article 104 vests executive authority in the President, including national-security policy, treaty ratification, appointment and dismissal of ministers and senior officials, military-use decisions, and presidential decrees subject to legal limits; Article 116 lets the TBMM or the President renew elections; Article 105 sets a parliamentary investigation path.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary constitutional text governing the 2022 presidency; direct and stable legal authority/constraint source.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Defines Erdoğan's office-level authority and checks in 2022; not a claim about personal conduct.
contrary_evidence: The same articles constrain decree power and preserve parliamentary/judicial checks.
Formal authority does not prove how he used it in practice.

evidence.claim: There were regular reports of torture and ill-treatment in police custody and prison, including severe beatings and cruel, inhuman, and degrading treatment, and prosecutors rarely investigated or prosecuted perpetrators.
evidence.title: World Report 2023: Turkey
evidence.excerpt: There were regular reports of torture and ill-treatment in police custody and prison, including severe beatings and cruel, inhuman, and degrading treatment, and prosecutors rarely investigated or prosecuted perpetrators.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Contemporary rights report synthesizing multiple cases and official inaction; strong for pattern evidence though not a court finding.
evidence.period_fit: Retrospective over 2022 and the surrounding period; useful for the 2022 domestic-safety environment.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Reflects institutions under Erdoğan in 2022, though it does not attribute every abuse to a direct presidential order.
contrary_evidence: The report notes some isolated investigations or trials, but says they were uncommon.
Some incidents are reported rather than adjudicated.

evidence.claim: Failure to enforce court protection orders leaves women open to continuing abuse from current or former husbands and partners, and some women were killed despite having obtained restraining orders intended to protect them.
evidence.title: Combatting Domestic Violence in Turkey: The Deadly Impact of Failure to Protect
evidence.excerpt: Failure to enforce court protection orders leaves women open to continuing abuse from current or former husbands and partners, and some women were killed despite having obtained restraining orders intended to protect them.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Detailed case-based investigation using complaints, court records, interviews, and 18 case files.
evidence.period_fit: Directly relevant to the 2019-2022 cases analyzed and published during 2022.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributes the protection gap to state institutions operating under Erdoğan's government, not to private abuse alone.
contrary_evidence: The report acknowledges protective orders exist in law.
It does not claim every domestic-violence case was politically directed from the center.

evidence.claim: Turkey's Interior Ministry estimated 307 women were killed in 2021 by men, and 38 had restraining orders issued for their protection at the time they were killed.
evidence.title: Turkey Fails Domestic Violence Victims
evidence.excerpt: Turkey's Interior Ministry estimated 307 women were killed in 2021 by men, and 38 had restraining orders issued for their protection at the time they were killed.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: HRW cites official Turkish data and uses it in a contemporary rights presentation; strong for scale and failure-to-protect context.
evidence.period_fit: Uses 2021 baseline but was published in 2022 and directly informs the 2022 domestic-safety environment.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Shows the protection problem persisted into Erdoğan's 2022 period, even if the killings themselves were committed by private perpetrators.
contrary_evidence: The figures are 2021 data, not a 2022-only count.
It is a rights-advocacy presentation rather than a government audit.

evidence.claim: The law increased punishments for intentional killing, injury, threat, torture, and torment when committed against women and limited discretionary sentence reductions.
evidence.title: Penalties Against the Acts of Violence Have Been Increased
evidence.publisher: Republic of Türkiye Ministry of Justice
evidence.excerpt: The law increased punishments for intentional killing, injury, threat, torture, and torment when committed against women and limited discretionary sentence reductions.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary official statement about enacted legal changes in 2022.
evidence.ruler_attribution: This is a ruler-era legal reform, though the Ministry frames it as a legislative measure rather than a personal act by Erdoğan alone.
contrary_evidence: The same evidence set shows weak enforcement and recurring protection failures.
A stronger statute does not prove effective implementation.

evidence.claim: Turkish police attacked and arrested hundreds of people at the Istanbul Pride March on June 26, 2022, and also arrested journalists reporting on the event.
evidence.title: Turkey: Mass Arrests, Anti-LGBT Violence at Pride
evidence.excerpt: Turkish police attacked and arrested hundreds of people at the Istanbul Pride March on June 26, 2022, and also arrested journalists reporting on the event.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Contemporaneous rights reporting with specific counts, dates, and event details.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributed to Turkish police under Erdoğan's government; the immediate street action was local police conduct, not an abstract national trend.
contrary_evidence: Local officials cited security and public-order reasons.
The report is rights-focused and not a full policing audit.

evidence.claim: Police violently broke up the student-organized Pride march at Middle East Technical University in Ankara on 10 June, detaining 37 students after dragging some of them on the ground.
evidence.title: Türkiye: Further information: Pride march dispersed with excessive force
evidence.excerpt: Police violently broke up the student-organized Pride march at Middle East Technical University in Ankara on 10 June, detaining 37 students after dragging some of them on the ground.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Direct contemporaneous human-rights reporting on a specific event with a clear date and casualty/detention count.
evidence.ruler_attribution: The conduct is attributed to Turkish police and the authorities allowing the crackdown; it does not show a presidential order by itself.
contrary_evidence: Authorities framed the event as a public-order issue.
The incident is a specific protest crackdown, not proof of nationwide mass terror.

evidence.claim: Turkish police blocked hundreds of people from gathering for Istanbul's annual Pride parade and detained dozens after local authorities banned the march.
evidence.title: Turkish police prevent Istanbul Pride from going ahead
evidence.excerpt: Turkish police blocked hundreds of people from gathering for Istanbul's annual Pride parade and detained dozens after local authorities banned the march.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Reuters dispatch is strong for event reporting and matches the HRW/Amnesty accounts.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributable to the state environment under Erdoğan, though the operational ban was issued by local authorities and carried out by police.
contrary_evidence: Local authorities said the march was banned for security reasons.
The piece reports the crackdown, not the full legal basis.

evidence.claim: Erdogan said a constitutional amendment would protect families from what he called 'perverse trends' and said he wanted to 'protect the family establishment' against LGBT-related change.
evidence.title: Erdogan says constitutional change will protect families against 'perverse trends'
evidence.excerpt: Erdogan said a constitutional amendment would protect families from what he called 'perverse trends' and said he wanted to 'protect the family establishment' against LGBT-related change.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Reuters reporting on a direct Erdoğan quotation; useful for ruler attribution even though republished by Yahoo.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Direct personal attribution to Erdoğan, not merely to subordinates or local police.
contrary_evidence: The speech was framed as family-protection politics by Erdoğan and AKP supporters.
It is rhetoric, not proof of a specific violent act.

evidence.claim: Reuters reported that critics saw Erdogan's constitutional-amendment push as targeting the LGBT+ community, and the article quoted him saying he aimed to protect the family from 'perverse trends'.
evidence.title: Erdogan moots putting Turkey headscarf reform to referendum
evidence.excerpt: Reuters reported that critics saw Erdogan's constitutional-amendment push as targeting the LGBT+ community, and the article quoted him saying he aimed to protect the family from 'perverse trends'.
evidence.source_locator: middle paragraphs on critics and quoted speech
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Reuters reporting ties the public speech to contemporaneous political effects and to the planned amendment debate.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Direct Erdoğan rhetoric, with the caveat that the constitutional change was still a proposal.
contrary_evidence: Supporters framed the proposal as protecting headscarf rights.
The link to LGBT targeting is an interpretive claim by critics, not an official admission.

evidence.claim: Turkey's interior minister said the blast on Istanbul's Istiklal Avenue killed six people and that police had detained 22 suspects, including the person who planted the bomb.
evidence.title: Turkey blames Istanbul blast on Kurdish militants, arrests 22, including bomber
evidence.excerpt: Turkey's interior minister said the blast on Istanbul's Istiklal Avenue killed six people and that police had detained 22 suspects, including the person who planted the bomb.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Reuters dispatch with concrete casualty and detention details about a major domestic security event.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributed to the Turkish state response under Erdoğan's government, though the immediate operational response ran through the interior ministry and police.
contrary_evidence: The source reports the government's claim about blame, not an independent forensic finding.
This is a crisis-response event, not a full accountability record.

unresolved_gaps: Direct 2022 nuclear-specific conduct is sparse; most positive evidence is alliance or humanitarian diplomacy rather than nuclear command, doctrine, or safety reform.
The package shows limited exposure and inherited NATO structure, but not a strong ruler-attributed improvement or deterioration in nuclear posture.

The package is strong on mediation and selective coercion, but weaker on independent verification of the civilian-harm allegations and on Erdoğan's own weighing of peaceful alternatives for the Syria/Iraq operations.
Several items are civic-space or press-repression evidence rather than direct physical-integrity harm, so the chapter partly relies on fear-climate inference.
Attribution for some harms is institutional rather than command-specific, especially for local policing and court actions.
There was no true 2022 succession or term-limit stress test, so the chapter relies on institutional erosion and media/election-law evidence instead of a direct transfer-of-power event.
Outcomes are heavily confounded by inflation shocks, external demand, the post-pandemic rebound, and CBRT formal independence, so causal credit remains partial.
Project-level delivery and regional/household distribution evidence are thinner than macro indicators.
The strongest welfare evidence is on health coverage and refugee cash transfers; housing, sanitation, and school-quality evidence is thinner.
Several positive items are donor-UNICEF/WHO partnerships, so Erdoğan attribution is meaningful but not exclusive.
There is no direct 2022 audited asset, gift, or procurement record for Erdoğan personally.
The strongest negative items are media-control and family-network allegations, not direct first-person dishonesty or self-dealing proof.
Project-level completion evidence is thin; the package shows allocation, program design, and some outcomes, but not audited delivery for specific 2022 initiatives.
Outcome attribution is still confounded by shocks and by private-sector behavior, especially on growth, exports, and labor-market statistics.
